lines.text: This chain jumps out of its jar. Nothing is pulling it up.
Drop the end of a long bead chain over the edge, and let gravity do the rest.
You'd expect it to slide over the rim, like a rope.
Instead it leaps up, and holds a steady arch above the jar.
And the drop sets the height. In our model, a one metre fall lifts the arch about fourteen centimetres.
Double the drop, and the arch doubles too.
From two metres up, the chain races along at almost five metres per second.
So what pushes it up? Not the falling chain. The pile itself.
A bead chain is made of short, stiff links. Lift one by its end, and it tips like a tiny lever.
Its other end digs into the pile, and the pile pushes back, upward.
A rope can't do that. It's floppy, so there's nothing to lever against the pile, and nothing throws it up.
That push helps throw every link up, so the chain shoots above the jar before gravity turns it around. A longer fall means a faster chain, and a harder push.
Physicists still argue about the details, like how much the beads bounce. But with no push from below, there's no fountain.
So the chain isn't pulled out of the jar. It's pushed, one link at a time.
